tip: Each verb takes its own 'mig' when you do something to yourself: 'tvättar mig' and 'klär på mig'.
'Inte' follows the first verb in a plain statement: 'kan inte simma', with the negation right after 'kan'.
'Brukar' plus a verb means usually or tend to: 'Jag brukar inte klaga' = I don't usually complain.
Laugh at something is 'skratta åt', not 'på' or 'till': 'skrattar åt skämtet' = laughs at the joke.
Swedish has no separate -ing form: 'springer' means both I run and I am running.
For things lying flat Swedish normally uses 'ligger', not 'är': 'Boken ligger i lådan' = the book is in the box.
Start a sentence with an adverb like 'faktiskt' and the verb comes before the subject: 'Faktiskt tycker jag'.
'Inte' splits the two-part verb 'tycka om': 'tycker inte om'. The 'om' belongs to the verb here.
'Inte ens' means not even, and sits between 'har' and 'försökt': 'har inte ens försökt'.
'Man' is a generic you or one, for people in general: 'ser man' = you see, one sees.
'Kunde' is the past of 'kan' (can): 'kunde inte hitta' = couldn't find.
With en-words, the -est form takes 'den' plus '-aste' plus the noun with its the-ending: 'den kallaste månaden'.
'Brukade' is the past of 'brukar' and means used to: 'brukade inte gilla' = didn't use to like.
Commands use the bare verb form with no pronoun: 'Sväng' = turn.
'Samma' takes a plain noun with no added ending: 'samma stad', not 'samma staden'.
'Hoppas' always ends in '-s' even though the meaning is active: 'Jag hoppas' = I hope.
Yes or no questions start with the verb: 'Ska vi ses...?' = Shall we meet...?
'Hem' is home as a direction you move toward; 'hemma' is home as a location: 'kommer hem' = come home.
Adjectives normally add '-t' with ett-words: 'ett stort hus'. On its own the word is 'stor'.
Most adjectives add '-are' for the -er form, and than is 'än': 'smutsigare än igår' = dirtier than yesterday.
For an equal comparison use 'lika' plus adjective plus 'som': 'lika bra som' = just as good as.
'Hur vill du betala': 'du' works for everyone since the 1960s du-reform, strangers and bosses alike.
'Sina' means their own and points back to the subject: 'sina grannar' = their own neighbors.
Longer adjectives usually take 'mer' instead of '-are': 'mer intressant' = more interesting.
'Kommer att' plus a verb means will; here 'det' slips inside: 'kommer det att snöa' = it will snow.
In a plain statement a word like 'alltid' (always) sits right after the verb: 'är alltid roligt'.
The '-s' ending makes the verb passive here: 'ses' = is seen or takes place, from 'se' (to see).
Tipping is not expected in Sweden – 'dricksen ingår' = the tip is included, service is usually in the price.
Comparatives usually add '-are': 'dyr' becomes 'dyrare' (more expensive). No separate word for more is needed.
'Ses' means see each other, the '-s' adding the each-other sense. 'Vi ses' is the everyday way to say see you later.
